articles.title: A forgotten fossil reveals a fearsome dinosaur with giant claws
articles.summary: A 120-million-year-old fossil forgotten in a museum for nearly a century has revealed a terrifying new dinosaur that may have been more dangerous to humans than a T. rex. The tiger-sized predator also provides the first evidence of megaraptorans in Europe, helping explain how these mysterious dinosaurs eventually became gigantic hunters.
articles.content:
A dinosaur fossil that spent nearly a century overlooked in a museum collection has turned out to belong to an entirely new species of prehistoric predator. About the size of a large tiger and armed with enormous curved claws, the animal roamed what is now Britain approximately 120 million years ago.

The discovery was made by researchers led by University College London (UCL), who examined a fossil skull fragment originally found on the Isle of Wight. Their findings, published in the journal Royal Society Open Science, identify the dinosaur as Invictibellatrix amberina, the first known European member of a mysterious group of carnivorous dinosaurs called megaraptorans.

These agile predators walked on two legs and were closely related to tyrannosaurs, including the famous Tyrannosaurus rex. However, their hunting equipment was strikingly different. Rather than relying primarily on massive jaws, megaraptorans had relatively narrow skulls, powerful arms, and huge curved claws that helped them seize their prey.

Some members of this group eventually became enormous predators, rivaling tyrannosaurs in size. Invictibellatrix, however, was among the earliest and smallest megaraptorans discovered so far.

Its name translates to "unconquered female warrior," a reference to the powerful predators that later emerged from this evolutionary lineage.

A Forgotten Dinosaur That Could Have Hunted Humans

The fossil consists of part of the rear of the dinosaur's skull. Although the Natural History Museum acquired it in 1924, its scientific importance went unrecognized for generations.

By comparing the fragment with fossils from related dinosaurs, researchers were able to estimate what this long-extinct animal might have looked like and how it lived.

Lead author Dr. Cassius Morrison (UCL Earth Sciences) said: "Based on what we know about its closest relatives, Invictibellatrix would have been three to four meters long and just over a meter and a half in height -- about as tall as a human. It would likely have had feathers and its claws might have been about 10cm to 20cm long. It would have eaten small dinosaurs, lizards and mammals -- occupying a similar role in the food chain to the hyena today.

"It was not the apex predator of its time, but for humans this dinosaur would have been more dangerous than a T. rex. We would have been perfectly sized prey, about a third of their body weight. They definitely would have chased us. A T. rex would not have bothered, as we would have been too small.

"It is a real mystery that this fossil was overlooked for so long, sitting in a drawer for nearly 100 years. Lots of bones are found on the Isle of Wight -- who knows what else is waiting to be discovered."

Although humans never encountered these dinosaurs, Morrison's comparison highlights an intriguing difference between predators of different sizes. A relatively small carnivore might have regarded a human as worthwhile prey, whereas an enormous hunter such as T. rex may have preferred much larger animals.

Discovery Solves a Mystery About Dinosaur Evolution

Beyond identifying a previously unknown species, the fossil provides an important missing piece in the evolutionary history of megaraptorans.

These dinosaurs remain among the least understood groups of large meat eaters because their fossils are exceptionally rare. Scientists have long suspected that they first evolved in Asia before spreading through Europe and eventually reaching the southern supercontinent of Gondwana (including present-day Africa, South America and Antarctica).

There was one major problem with that explanation: Until now, no megaraptoran fossils had been identified in Europe.

The discovery of Invictibellatrix provides the evidence researchers needed to support that proposed migration route.

Co-author Charlie Scherer, a PhD student at UCL Earth Sciences, said: "This new species is the first proof we have that megaraptorans were also present in Europe and that they reached Gondwana this way rather than island-hopping further south."

The finding suggests that Europe was an important part of the journey that eventually brought these predators to the southern continents, where some of their descendants became dominant hunters.

CT Scans Reveal the Dinosaur's Hidden Anatomy

To determine exactly what kind of dinosaur they were examining, the scientists used CT scanning technology to investigate the fossil in detail.

The scans allowed them to build a three-dimensional reconstruction of the skull fragment, along with a model of its internal cavity. This provided clues about the shape of the space that once housed the dinosaur's brain.

The team then compared its anatomy with fossils from several other groups of meat-eating dinosaurs, including tyrannosaurs, spinosaurs, raptors, and other predators that walked on two legs.

Several unusual features helped distinguish the specimen from known species. These included an oval opening where the spinal cord connected to the brain and a distinctive crest shaped like an hourglass.

Together, these anatomical characteristics indicated that the fossil represented a previously unidentified dinosaur.

The researchers also used computer algorithms to compare its skeletal features with those of other dinosaurs. These analyses consistently placed Invictibellatrix within the megaraptoran group, providing further support for the identification.

How Giant Megaraptors Conquered the Southern Continents

The team went beyond examining the fossil itself, using mathematical models to reconstruct how megaraptorans spread and evolved over millions of years.

Their analysis combined the available fossil record with evolutionary relationships among dinosaurs, ancient geography, and climate conditions.

The results suggest that megaraptorans were distributed widely around the world during the Early Cretaceous (i.e., at the time of Invictibellatrix).

However, their fortunes appear to have changed dramatically as the Cretaceous continued.

By the Late Cretaceous, tens of millions of years later, megaraptorans had probably disappeared from the northern supercontinent of Laurasia (including modern-day Europe).

In the south, the story was very different. Megaraptorans continued evolving across Gondwana, eventually becoming some of the largest and most formidable predators in their ecosystems.

Some developed claws measuring up to 35cm (14") long. One particularly impressive example, Maip macrothorax, lived in what is now Argentina and is estimated to have reached nine to 10 meters in length, with a body weight comparable to that of an elephant.

Exactly why megaraptorans apparently vanished from northern regions remains uncertain. The researchers suggest several possibilities, including changes in climate, shifts in environmental conditions, and competition from other large carnivorous dinosaurs such as tyrannosaurs.

A Century-Old Museum Fossil Finally Reveals Its Secret

The fossil that made this discovery possible was originally collected by amateur paleontologist Reginald Walter Tooley near the base of a cliff on the southwestern coast of the Isle of Wight.

Tooley discovered more than 1,000 fossil specimens during his lifetime. Following his death, the Natural History Museum acquired his collection, including the skull fragment that would eventually be identified as Invictibellatrix.

The discovery highlights how important fossils can remain unrecognized even after spending decades in museum collections.

Professor Paul Barrett, the study's senior author from the Natural History Museum, said: "Despite over 200 years of collecting, the Isle of Wight continues to surprise us with new dinosaur species, and finds of carnivorous dinosaurs, such as Invictibellatrix, have been particularly elusive.

"Work like this shows the exceptional value of working with historical museum collections where there are still many discoveries to be made."

The researchers also gave the dinosaur's name a deeper meaning.

In their paper, they explained that Invictibellatrix was chosen to "give hope and strength to all those who are bullied, discriminated, victimized, and oppressed that tomorrow will be theirs and not to give up in face of such odds."

The second part of its name, amberina, honors both the amber found in the rock layers where the fossil originated and the female name Amberina.

The study received funding from the Palaeontographical Society, the Royal Society, and UKRI.

With a single forgotten skull fragment revealing an entirely new dinosaur and helping reconstruct the ancient movements of giant predators, the findings demonstrate that some of paleontology's most intriguing discoveries may already be sitting in museum drawers, waiting for someone to take a closer look.
articles.reasoning: The discovery of a new dinosaur species from a century-old fossil provides significant scientific insight into dinosaur evolution and migration, revealing the first evidence of megaraptorans in Europe. This finding has broad implications for paleontology and our understanding of prehistoric life, representing a meaningful advancement in knowledge with inspiring potential for future discoveries.
articles.personality_title: Forgotten fossil reveals new dinosaur species with giant claws in Europe
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – A dinosaur fossil found on the Isle of Wight in Britain was stored in a museum for nearly 100 years without being studied closely. Scientists recently took another look and discovered it belonged to a new kind of dinosaur that lived about 120 million years ago.

**What happened** – Researchers from University College London studied a skull fragment of this dinosaur, named Invictibellatrix amberina. This tiger-sized predator had large curved claws and walked on two legs. It is the first evidence of megaraptorans, a group of carnivorous dinosaurs, living in Europe. The fossil was originally found in 1924 but only recently recognized as a new species.

**Impact** – This discovery is important because it fills a gap in our knowledge about how megaraptorans spread across the world. Until now, scientists thought these dinosaurs only lived in Asia and the southern continents. Finding one in Europe shows they traveled through this region before reaching places like South America. It also suggests this smaller predator might have been more dangerous to humans than the famous T. rex because of its size and hunting style.

**What's next step** – Scientists hope to examine more fossils from the Isle of Wight and other places to find additional megaraptorans or new species. They also plan to use advanced imaging and computer models to learn more about how these dinosaurs evolved and moved across ancient continents.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A century-old fossil has revealed a new European dinosaur species with giant claws, changing what we know about dinosaur migration and evolution.
articles.personality_title_fr: Un fossile oublié révèle une nouvelle espèce de dinosaure aux griffes géantes en Europe
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Un fossile de dinosaure trouvé sur l’île de Wight en Grande-Bretagne a été conservé dans un musée pendant près de 100 ans sans être étudié en détail. Les scientifiques l’ont récemment examiné de nouveau et ont découvert qu’il appartenait à un nouveau type de dinosaure ayant vécu il y a environ 120 millions d’années.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des chercheurs du University College London ont étudié un fragment de crâne de ce dinosaure, nommé Invictibellatrix amberina. Ce prédateur de la taille d’un tigre avait de grandes griffes courbées et marchait sur deux pattes. C’est la première preuve de la présence de mégaraptorans, un groupe de dinosaures carnivores, en Europe. Le fossile avait été trouvé en 1924 mais n’avait été reconnu comme une nouvelle espèce que récemment.

**Impact** – Cette découverte est importante car elle comble un vide dans nos connaissances sur la façon dont les mégaraptorans se sont répandus dans le monde. Jusqu’à présent, on pensait que ces dinosaures vivaient seulement en Asie et dans les continents du Sud. En trouver un en Europe montre qu’ils ont traversé cette région avant d’atteindre des endroits comme l’Amérique du Sud. Cela suggère aussi que ce prédateur plus petit aurait pu être plus dangereux pour les humains que le célèbre T. rex, à cause de sa taille et de sa façon de chasser.

**Étape suivante** – Les scientifiques espèrent examiner plus de fossiles de l’île de Wight et d’autres endroits pour trouver d’autres mégaraptorans ou de nouvelles espèces. Ils prévoient aussi d’utiliser des images avancées et des modèles informatiques pour mieux comprendre comment ces dinosaures ont évolué et se sont déplacés sur les continents anciens.

**Conclusion en une phrase** – Un fossile vieux d’un siècle a révélé une nouvelle espèce européenne de dinosaure aux griffes géantes, changeant notre compréhension de la migration et de l’évolution des dinosaures.
articles.personality_title_es: Un fósil olvidado revela una nueva especie de dinosaurio con garras gigantes en Europa
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Un fósil de dinosaurio encontrado en la Isla de Wight, en Gran Bretaña, estuvo guardado en un museo durante casi 100 años sin ser estudiado profundamente. Recientemente, los científicos lo examinaron de nuevo y descubrieron que pertenecía a un nuevo tipo de dinosaurio que vivió hace unos 120 millones de años.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores de University College London estudiaron un fragmento de cráneo de este dinosaurio, llamado Invictibellatrix amberina. Este depredador del tamaño de un tigre tenía grandes garras curvadas y caminaba sobre dos patas. Es la primera evidencia de megarraptores, un grupo de dinosaurios carnívoros, en Europa. El fósil fue encontrado en 1924 pero solo recientemente se identificó como una nueva especie.

**Impacto** – Este descubrimiento es importante porque completa un vacío en nuestro conocimiento sobre cómo se dispersaron los megarraptores por el mundo. Hasta ahora, se pensaba que estos dinosaurios solo vivían en Asia y en los continentes del sur. Encontrar uno en Europa muestra que viajaron por esta región antes de llegar a lugares como Sudamérica. También sugiere que este depredador más pequeño podría haber sido más peligroso para los humanos que el famoso T. rex debido a su tamaño y estilo de caza.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos esperan examinar más fósiles de la Isla de Wight y otros lugares para encontrar más megarraptores o nuevas especies. También planean usar imágenes avanzadas y modelos computarizados para aprender más sobre cómo evolucionaron estos dinosaurios y se movieron por los continentes antiguos.

**Resumen en una frase** – Un fósil olvidado de hace un siglo ha revelado una nueva especie europea de dinosaurio con garras gigantes, cambiando lo que sabemos sobre la migración y evolución de los dinosaurios.

articles.title: Ancient shipwreck discovered off Turkey claimed to be world’s oldest
articles.summary: A ship that sank in the Early Bronze Age was probably carrying jars of olive oil and may have been on its way to the ancient city of Troy when it sank
articles.content:
A ship that sank in the Early Bronze Age was probably carrying jars of olive oil and may have been on its way to the ancient city of Troy when it sank

This shipwreck might date from the Early Bronze Age Hakan Oniz/Akdeniz University

An ancient shipwreck found off the southern coast of Turkey may be around 4500 years old. That makes it the oldest shipwreck ever found, says Hakan Öniz at Akdeniz University in Antalya, Turkey, who led the team that discovered it.

The archaeologists first saw the shipwreck near Kekova Island in 2024, during an underwater survey along Turkey’s Mediterranean coast. The wood of the wreck itself has long since decomposed, but in excavations completed earlier this month, they retrieved its cargo – around 30 storage jars called amphoras – from the seabed.

The amphoras from the Kekova shipwreck have a distinctive shape with side handles and flat bases, similar to other pottery from the Levant and Egypt that dates to the Early Bronze Age. This enabled the researchers to date them to between 2700 and 2400 BC. It’s an insight into the earliest period of Mediterranean maritime trade, says Öniz. As international trade became established, traders switched to jars with tapered, “carrot-shaped” bottoms, because they pack more efficiently onto ships.

Advertisement

Minor variations between the amphoras suggest that they came from “different workshops and probably different settlements”, says Öniz. He concludes from the cargo that the ship was about 10 metres long, and departed from a harbour along the eastern Mediterranean coast. The crew would then have sailed along the coast, picking up amphoras filled with olive oil or wine from different villages. They were probably taking them to the Minoan civilisation on Crete, or to the city of Troy, in north-western Turkey, when the ship sank.

As well as the amphoras, the archaeologists found several stone anchors. These were lying some distance from the wreck, suggesting they may have been thrown overboard when the ship got into difficulty during a storm. The wreck lies about 30 metres down, says Öniz, on a particularly treacherous stretch of coast that is plagued by strong currents and winds.

Hundreds of ancient shipwrecks have been found along Turkey’s Mediterranean coast. Most of them sank during the Roman and Byzantine periods, but a handful have been dated to the Bronze Age. The Uluburun wreck, for example, discovered in 1982 is from the Late Bronze Age. It sank around 1300 BC, carrying treasures including ebony, ivory, ostrich eggs and jewellery from cultures across the Mediterranean world. In recent surveys, Öniz has found another two Bronze Age wrecks, one dating from the Middle Bronze Age and one from the Early Bronze Age. But Kekova appears to be the oldest yet found.

It’s “a fascinating and potentially very important discovery”, says Jon Henderson at the University of Edinburgh, UK. But he cautions that he’d like to see published evidence before “crowning it the world’s oldest shipwreck”, noting that dating by pottery comparisons isn’t always very accurate, because similar forms and decorative features can occur over quite long periods. Radiocarbon data would help to pin down the date, but unfortunately no organic material survives at the site.

Until now, the world’s oldest known shipwreck was an Early Bronze Age wreck at Dokos in southern Greece, dated to 2700-2200 BC. Öniz argues that Kekova is older than Dokos, but the two wrecks could actually be contemporary, says Henderson.

“What really excites me isn’t whether this wreck is a century or two older than another one,” he adds. “It’s that we’re looking at a snapshot of Mediterranean maritime trade more than 4000 years ago.”

We know people were moving goods across the sea at this time, “but finding physical remains of this is extraordinarily rare”, says Henderson.
articles.reasoning: The discovery of the potentially oldest shipwreck offers significant insight into early Mediterranean maritime trade, revealing tangible evidence of ancient human activity and cultural exchange from over 4000 years ago. This archaeological find has broad historical and cultural significance, providing a meaningful contribution to our understanding of early civilizations and their interactions.
articles.personality_title: Ancient shipwreck off Turkey may be the world’s oldest
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Archaeologists have been exploring the Mediterranean coast of Turkey, an area known for many ancient shipwrecks. Most wrecks found there are from later historical periods, but some date back to the Bronze Age, a time over 4,000 years ago when early civilizations were trading goods by sea.

**What happened** – In 2024, a team led by Hakan Öniz from Akdeniz University discovered a shipwreck near Kekova Island. The ship sank during the Early Bronze Age, about 4,500 years ago. Though the wooden ship has decayed, researchers recovered about 30 clay jars called amphoras from the seabed. These jars likely held olive oil or wine and came from different villages along the eastern Mediterranean coast. Stone anchors found nearby suggest the ship may have sunk during a storm.

**Impact** – This shipwreck could be the oldest ever found, offering a rare glimpse into early sea trade. The jars’ style helped date the wreck and showed how people exchanged goods like olive oil around 2700 to 2400 BC. Finding physical remains like these is unusual and helps us understand how ancient cultures connected across the Mediterranean, possibly including places like Troy and Crete.

**What's next step** – Researchers hope to confirm the exact age of the wreck with more scientific tests, though the lack of organic material makes this difficult. They will also continue studying other Bronze Age wrecks to learn more about early maritime trade and how ancient people moved goods by sea.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The discovery of a 4,500-year-old shipwreck off Turkey reveals valuable evidence of some of the earliest sea trade in the Mediterranean, deepening our knowledge of ancient civilizations’ connections.
articles.personality_title_fr: Une épave ancienne en Turquie pourrait être la plus vieille du monde
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Des archéologues explorent la côte méditerranéenne de la Turquie, une région connue pour de nombreuses épaves anciennes. La plupart des épaves découvertes datent de périodes historiques plus récentes, mais certaines remontent à l’âge du bronze, il y a plus de 4 000 ans, lorsque les premières civilisations commerçaient par la mer.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – En 2024, une équipe dirigée par Hakan Öniz de l’Université Akdeniz a découvert une épave près de l’île de Kekova. Le navire a coulé pendant l’Âge du bronze ancien, il y a environ 4 500 ans. Bien que le bois du navire se soit décomposé, les chercheurs ont récupéré environ 30 jarres en argile appelées amphores sur le fond marin. Ces jarres contenaient probablement de l’huile d’olive ou du vin et venaient de différents villages de la côte méditerranéenne orientale. Des ancres en pierre trouvées à proximité suggèrent que le navire a pu sombrer lors d’une tempête.

**Impact** – Cette épave pourrait être la plus vieille jamais trouvée, offrant un aperçu rare du commerce maritime ancien. Le style des jarres a aidé à dater l’épave et montre comment les gens échangeaient des biens comme l’huile d’olive entre 2700 et 2400 av. J.-C. Trouver des vestiges physiques comme ceux-ci est inhabituel et aide à comprendre comment les cultures anciennes étaient reliées à travers la Méditerranée, peut-être entre Troie et la Crète.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs espèrent confirmer l’âge exact de l’épave avec d’autres tests scientifiques, même si le manque de matière organique complique cette tâche. Ils continueront aussi à étudier d’autres épaves de l’âge du bronze pour en apprendre davantage sur le commerce maritime ancien et le transport des marchandises par la mer.

**Résumé en une phrase** – La découverte d’une épave vieille de 4 500 ans en Turquie révèle des preuves précieuses du commerce maritime le plus ancien en Méditerranée, enrichissant notre compréhension des liens entre les civilisations anciennes.
articles.personality_title_es: Un naufragio antiguo en Turquía podría ser el más viejo del mundo
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Arqueólogos han estado explorando la costa mediterránea de Turquía, un área conocida por muchos naufragios antiguos. La mayoría de los naufragios encontrados son de períodos históricos posteriores, pero algunos datan de la Edad del Bronce, hace más de 4,000 años, cuando las primeras civilizaciones comerciaban por mar.

**Qué pasó** – En 2024, un equipo liderado por Hakan Öniz de la Universidad Akdeniz descubrió un naufragio cerca de la isla Kekova. El barco se hundió durante la Edad del Bronce Temprano, hace aproximadamente 4,500 años. Aunque la madera del barco se ha descompuesto, los investigadores recuperaron unas 30 vasijas de barro llamadas ánforas del fondo marino. Estas vasijas probablemente contenían aceite de oliva o vino y provenían de diferentes pueblos a lo largo de la costa este del Mediterráneo. Se encontraron anclas de piedra cerca, lo que sugiere que el barco pudo hundirse durante una tormenta.

**Impacto** – Este naufragio podría ser el más antiguo encontrado, ofreciendo una mirada rara al comercio marítimo temprano. El estilo de las vasijas ayudó a fechar el naufragio y mostró cómo la gente intercambiaba productos como el aceite de oliva entre 2700 y 2400 a.C. Encontrar restos físicos como estos es inusual y ayuda a entender cómo las culturas antiguas estaban conectadas a través del Mediterráneo, posiblemente incluyendo lugares como Troya y Creta.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores esperan confirmar la edad exacta del naufragio con más pruebas científicas, aunque la falta de material orgánico dificulta esto. También continuarán estudiando otros naufragios de la Edad del Bronce para aprender más sobre el comercio marítimo temprano y cómo las personas movían mercancías por mar.

**Resumen en una frase** – El descubrimiento de un naufragio de 4,500 años frente a Turquía revela evidencia valiosa del comercio marítimo más antiguo en el Mediterráneo, aumentando nuestro conocimiento sobre las conexiones de las civilizaciones antiguas.
